free.g1m-2020-p2-1a:
Town planningCitadel and lower townDrainage systemStandardisation

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) was India's first urban culture, the Bronze Age "first urbanisation". Excavations at Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R.D. Banerji, 1922), Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi reveal a remarkable degree of civic planning: planned streets, standard bricks, covered drains and public buildings, spread over a vast area, yet without any clearly identified palace or temple.

1. Layout of the city

  • Grid pattern: main streets ran north–south and east–west, crossing at right angles and dividing the town into rectangular blocks; narrow lanes led into the residential quarters.
  • Two-part division: a raised, fortified citadel on the west held public buildings, while a larger lower town on the east housed the people. Dholavira had a three-fold division into citadel, middle town and lower town.
  • Zoning of activities: bead-making workshops at Lothal and Chanhudaro and circular working floors near the granaries of Harappa suggest planned use of space.

2. Buildings and materials

  • Standardised bricks: burnt bricks in the uniform ratio 1:2:4 were used across a huge area, showing common standards of measurement; Kalibangan used mud bricks and Dholavira mainly stone.
  • Houses: one or two storeys built around courtyards, with wells, bathrooms and kitchens; doors opened into side lanes rather than main streets, ensuring privacy.
  • Public structures: the Great Bath (about 12 m × 7 m × 2.4 m) at Mohenjo-daro, made watertight with a layer of bitumen; granaries at Harappa; the dockyard at Lothal; and the stone reservoirs of Dholavira.

3. Sanitation and water management

  • Covered drainage: house drains joined brick-lined street drains with manholes and soak pits, among the most advanced systems of the Bronze Age world.
  • Water supply: Mohenjo-daro had several hundred wells, while Dholavira stored rain and stream water in a chain of rock-cut reservoirs in the dry Kutch region.
  • Civic discipline: regular cleaning of drains and disposal of refuse imply some form of municipal authority.

4. A critical view

  • Uniformity exaggerated: Lothal had a single enclosing wall, Kalibangan fortified both parts and Banawali's streets were not on a grid, so there was no single template.
  • Debated functions: whether the "granary" was a granary or an assembly hall, and the "dockyard" a dock or a water tank, is still discussed.
  • Decline: in the late phase, houses at Mohenjo-daro encroached on streets and building quality fell, showing weakening civic control.
  • Unknown authority: with no palaces or royal tombs, it is unclear whether priests, merchants or a council planned and enforced civic rules.

Harappan planning thus combined standardisation, sanitation and zoning on a scale unmatched in its age, even if it was less uniform than once believed. Dholavira's inscription as a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021) shows its global value, and its water harvesting and drainage still offer lessons for planned cities such as Amaravati.
free.g1m-2023-p2-1a:
Harappan continuityMaterial cultureProto-Hindu beliefsSubstratum of Indian civilization

The Harappan Civilization (mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE) declined as a city culture, but it did not vanish. Its farming, crafts, beliefs and customs passed through Late Harappan and Chalcolithic village cultures into Vedic and later Indian life. Much of this inheritance survives today in villages, temples and households, so the Harappan world forms the substratum of Indian civilization rather than a dead past.

1. Town planning and technology

  • Planned settlements: grid-pattern streets, covered drains and soak pits at Mohenjodaro and Harappa anticipate the drainage and sanitation principles of modern town planning.
  • Water management: the reservoirs of Dholavira and the Great Bath foreshadow the stepwells and temple tanks of later India.
  • Weights and measures: cubical chert weights followed a binary system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16…); the 16-anna rupee, used until decimal coinage in 1957, follows the same logic.
  • Transport: terracotta models of bullock carts and boats closely resemble the carts and boats still used in Sindh, Rajasthan and Gujarat.

2. Economy and crafts

  • Agriculture: the criss-cross furrowed field at Kalibangan resembles the mixed cropping still practised in Rajasthan.
  • Cotton: the Harappans were among the earliest people to grow cotton; cotton textiles remain a hallmark of Indian craft.
  • Crafts: carnelian bead-making (still practised at Khambhat), black-on-red pottery and the potter's wheel continue in village crafts.

3. Religion and beliefs

  • Mother Goddess: numerous female figurines anticipate Shakti worship and village goddess cults.
  • Proto-Shiva: John Marshall read the 'Pashupati' seal, a horned figure in a yogic posture surrounded by animals, as proto-Shiva; linga–yoni stones point the same way.
  • Nature worship: the sacred pipal, the humped bull and the swastika remain objects of veneration.
  • Ritual: fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal, and ritual bathing at the Great Bath, echo Vedic sacrifices and the Hindu emphasis on purificatory bathing.

4. Social customs and daily life

  • Ornaments: the bronze 'dancing girl' wears many bangles; red pigment in the hair-parting of figurines at Nausharo resembles sindoor (J.M. Kenoyer's interpretation).
  • Leisure and homes: dice, toy carts, whistles and courtyard houses with rooms opening inward survive in village life.

5. Limits of continuity

  • Lost elements: the script, standardised town planning and trade with Mesopotamia disappeared; cities returned only with the second urbanisation of the 6th century BCE.
  • Caveat: as the script is undeciphered, religious continuities are inferences from archaeology, not certainties.

AP angle: the mother-goddess cult lives on in AP's village goddesses (gramadevatas) such as Gangamma and Poleramma, and bullock carts and courtyard houses remain common in rural Andhra.

Thus Harappan culture survives less in monuments than in everyday practices, a striking example of continuity amid change in Indian civilization.
free.g1m-2023-p2-1b:
Chinese pilgrimsFa-Hien and Hiuen-TsangGupta and Harsha administrationBuddhist bias

Chinese Buddhist pilgrims came to India to visit the sacred places of the Buddha and to collect texts. Fa-Hien's Fo-kuo-ki (early 5th century), Hiuen-Tsang's Si-yu-ki (7th century) and I-Tsing's record of Buddhist practice (late 7th century) are dated, first-hand outsider sources on Gupta and post-Gupta India, though coloured by their Buddhist outlook.

1. Socio-religious life

  • Diet and customs (Fa-Hien): the people of Madhyadesha were prosperous; most avoided meat, liquor, onion and garlic, no pigs or fowls were kept, and cowries served as money in markets.
  • Untouchability: Fa-Hien saw Chandalas living outside towns and striking a piece of wood to announce their approach; Hiuen-Tsang found butchers, fishermen and scavengers living outside settlements, showing a hardening of caste.
  • Varna and learning (Hiuen-Tsang): he describes the four varnas and Brahmana vegetarianism, and Nalanda as a great centre with thousands of students, where he himself studied under Silabhadra.
  • Religion: Fa-Hien found Buddhism flourishing alongside Brahmanism; by Hiuen-Tsang's time Buddhism was declining in many regions. Harsha's quinquennial assembly at Prayag honoured the Buddha, Surya and Shiva.
  • Monastic life (I-Tsing): after about ten years at Nalanda, he described the vinaya discipline, the curriculum, Sanskrit grammar, medicine, diet and the hygiene of monks.

2. Administration

  • Gupta mildness (Fa-Hien): no registration of households; crimes were punished mostly by fines, with the cutting off of the right hand only for repeated rebellion; free hospitals and rest-houses existed at Pataliputra.
  • Harsha's revenue (Hiuen-Tsang): taxation was light, about one-sixth of the produce; revenue from crown lands was divided into four parts: for state affairs, for public servants, for scholars and for religious gifts.
  • Officials and labour: officials were paid by assignments of land, and forced labour was limited and paid.
  • Law and order: punishments were harsher than in Gupta times (mutilation and ordeals by water, fire, weighing and poison), and roads were unsafe; Hiuen-Tsang himself was robbed.

AP angle: Hiuen-Tsang visited Andhra (around Vengi) and Dhanakataka (the Amaravati region) and found many Buddhist monasteries, most of them deserted, evidence of Buddhism's decline in its old Andhra heartland.

3. Value and limitations

  • Value: precise dates and first-hand detail fill gaps in Indian texts; Hiuen-Tsang's descriptions later helped archaeologists identify Buddhist sites.
  • Limitations: a Buddhist bias, little political history, generalisations from short stays, and problems with Indian languages and names.

Read with inscriptions and Bana's Harshacharita, these accounts remain indispensable for reconstructing the society and governance of early India.
free.g1m-2025-p2-1a:
Harappan urbanismMehrgarhIndigenous originSpatial expansion

The Indus Valley or Harappan Civilization was South Asia's first urban culture, with a mature phase of about 2600–1900 BCE. It came to light when Daya Ram Sahni excavated Harappa (1921) and R.D. Banerji excavated Mohenjo-daro (1922). Planned cities, standard weights, seals and an undeciphered script show a highly organised society. Its origin and spread are best understood through its Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases.

1. Origin: two views

  • Diffusionist view: Mortimer Wheeler and Gordon Childe argued that the idea of city life came from Mesopotamia, pointing to trade contacts and some shared traits.
  • Indigenous evolution (now accepted): excavations at Mehrgarh in Baluchistan (J.-F. Jarrige) show farming villages from about 7000 BCE, with wheat, barley, cattle and mud-brick houses, growing step by step towards urban life.
  • Early Harappan phase (c. 3200–2600 BCE): sites such as Amri, Kot Diji, Kalibangan and Rehman Dheri already had fortifications, wheel-made pottery and planned layouts, the direct ancestors of the mature cities.
  • Distinctiveness: the script, seals, grid planning and covered drains have no Mesopotamian model, and the Rakhigarhi ancient-DNA study (2019) traced Harappan ancestry largely to local populations.

2. Expansion and extent

  • Area: the civilization covered about 1.3 million sq km, larger than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia.
  • Core along rivers: major cities followed the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra — Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan and Banawali.
  • Coastal Gujarat: Lothal (with its dockyard), Dholavira (with its water reservoirs) and Surkotada linked the civilization to sea trade.
  • Frontiers: Manda in the north, Daimabad in the south, Sutkagen-dor in the west and Alamgirpur in the east; Shortughai in Afghanistan was a trading outpost.

3. Drivers of expansion

  • Fertile floodplains: farming of wheat and barley on river floodplains produced a surplus to feed cities, craftsmen and traders.
  • Trade and raw materials: copper from Khetri, lapis lazuli from Badakhshan, and shell and carnelian from Gujarat; Mesopotamian texts call the region "Meluhha".
  • Standardisation: bricks in the ratio 1:2:4, uniform weights and seals sustained a common economic system across distant regions.
  • Later shift: after about 1900 BCE, as rivers changed course and trade declined (the causes are debated), Late Harappan settlements moved east into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and south into Gujarat and Maharashtra.

AP angle: Andhra lay outside the Harappan zone; it was then home to Neolithic farming and cattle-herding communities of the southern Deccan, with remains at sites such as Nagarjunakonda.

The Harappan Civilization was thus an indigenous growth that expanded along rivers and trade routes. Ongoing work at Rakhigarhi and Dholavira (a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021) keeps refining this picture.
free.g1m-2025-p2-1b:
Shramana traditionFour Noble TruthsTriratnaAhimsa

In the 6th–5th centuries BCE, the Gangetic valley saw the growth of cities, trade and a shramana (ascetic) reaction against costly Vedic sacrifices, ritualism and Brahmanical dominance. Gautama Buddha and Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Jain Tirthankara, gave this protest its most lasting form. Both offered liberation through ethical conduct rather than ritual, and both preached in the people's languages, Pali and Ardhamagadhi.

1. Teachings of Buddha

  • Four Noble Truths: life is full of suffering (dukkha); desire (tanha) is its cause; suffering can end; and the way to end it is the Eightfold Path.
  • Ashtangika Marga (Middle Path): right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration, avoiding both luxury and harsh austerity.
  • Philosophy: dependent origination (pratityasamutpada), impermanence (anicca) and no permanent soul (anatta); karma decides rebirth, and the goal is nirvana.
  • Social message: silent on God; rejected Vedic authority, animal sacrifice and caste; opened the sangha to all, including women.

2. Teachings of Mahavira

  • Triratna: right faith, right knowledge and right conduct lead to liberation (kaivalya) from the cycle of birth.
  • Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya and aparigraha came from Parshvanatha, and Mahavira added brahmacharya; monks keep them strictly as mahavratas, lay followers as milder anuvratas.
  • Soul in everything: even stones, plants and water have a soul (jiva); hence extreme non-violence, fasting and austerity.
  • Anekantavada and syadvada: truth has many sides and can be stated only conditionally, a philosophy of tolerance.
  • Attitude to authority: rejected the Vedas and a creator God, but criticised varna less sharply than Buddhism.

3. Analysis: common ground and differences

  • Common ground: both were Kshatriya teachers who rejected ritualism, Vedic authority and priestly monopoly, and stressed karma, rebirth and moral conduct.
  • Differences: Buddha's Middle Path was practical, while Mahavira demanded rigorous austerity; Buddhism denied a permanent soul, Jainism saw souls everywhere.
  • Spread: Buddhism's missionary sangha and royal patronage (Ashoka) made it a world religion; Jainism's rigour kept it smaller but enduring among merchants.
  • Social appeal: both attracted the new merchant class, and their ethics of non-violence suited trade and settled farming.

AP angle: Buddhism flourished at Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda and Bhattiprolu, and Acharya Nagarjuna developed the Madhyamika philosophy; Jain remains survive at Ramatheertham (Vizianagaram) and Danavulapadu (YSR Kadapa).

Their message of ahimsa, tolerance and self-discipline inspired Ashoka's dhamma and Gandhi's satyagraha, and it remains relevant in an age of conflict and excessive consumption.
free.g1m-2020-p3-1a:
Constituent AssemblyCabinet Mission PlanBag of borrowingsConstitutionalism

The idea of a Constituent Assembly was first put forward by M.N. Roy (1934); the Congress officially demanded one in 1935, and the British accepted the demand in principle in the August Offer (1940). The Assembly was finally constituted in November 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan. In just under three years it framed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949, whose merits and flaws have been debated ever since.

1. Formation of the Constituent Assembly

  • Strength: a total of 389 seats: 296 for British India (292 from the eleven governors' provinces and 4 from the chief commissioners' provinces) and 93 for the princely states.
  • Allocation: seats were shared among the provinces and princely states roughly in proportion to population (about one seat per ten lakh people) and divided among the General, Muslim and Sikh communities.
  • Indirect election: members of the provincial assemblies elected the representatives by proportional representation through the single transferable vote in July–August 1946. The Congress won 208 seats, the Muslim League 73 and small groups and independents 15; princely-state members were to be nominated by the rulers.
  • Working: it first met on 9 December 1946 (the League boycotted it), elected Dr Rajendra Prasad President and set up the Drafting Committee under Dr B.R. Ambedkar on 29 August 1947. After Partition its strength fell to 299.
  • Andhra members: Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar (Drafting Committee), N.G. Ranga, Durgabai Deshmukh and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.

2. Strengths of the Constitution as framed

  • Democratic content: universal adult franchise from the very first general election, a bold step for a poor and largely non-literate new nation.
  • Rights with remedies: justiciable Fundamental Rights backed by Article 32, which Ambedkar called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, and Directive Principles to guide a welfare state.
  • Social revolution: abolition of untouchability (Art 17) and safeguards for SCs, STs and minorities; Granville Austin called it "first and foremost a social document".
  • Balanced institutions: parliamentary government, an independent judiciary and a federation with a strong Centre suited to a newly partitioned country.

3. Criticisms and the counter-view

These criticisms are only partly valid. Decisions were taken by consensus and accommodation rather than by majority votes, and the drafts were openly debated clause by clause.

In conclusion, the Assembly's legitimacy rests less on how it was elected than on what it produced: a democratic, rights-based Constitution that has endured for over 75 years. As Ambedkar warned, its success depends on those who work it, that is, on constitutional morality.
free.g1m-2020-p3-1b:
Judicial reviewBasic structureArticle 13Separation of powers

Judicial review is the power of the courts to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders of both the Centre and the States, and to declare them void if they violate the Constitution. Born in Marbury v. Madison (USA, 1803), it rests in India on Articles 13, 32 and 226 (with Arts 131–136 and 245–246). It is part of the basic structure of the Constitution (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997), so even Parliament cannot take it away.

1. Justice S.S.M. Quadri's classification

Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri classified judicial review into three categories:

  • Constitutional amendments: Parliament's amending power is wide but not unlimited; amendments that destroy core features such as judicial independence or free elections can be struck down.
  • Legislation: laws are tested against Part III and the division of powers; even Ninth Schedule laws placed there after 24 April 1973 are reviewable (I.R. Coelho, 2007).
  • Administrative action: executive decisions are tested for illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety and, increasingly, proportionality.

2. Scope of judicial review

  • Three grounds: a law or order can be struck down if it infringes Fundamental Rights, lies outside the competence of the authority that framed it, or is repugnant to any other constitutional provision.
  • Judicial doctrines: severability, eclipse, pith and substance, harmonious construction and colourable legislation guide the courts.
  • Narrower than in the USA: Article 21 uses "procedure established by law", not American "due process"; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened it by requiring procedure to be "fair, just and reasonable".
  • Limits: courts show restraint on economic policy (BALCO, 2002) and political questions.

3. Importance of judicial review

  • Supremacy of the Constitution: every organ must act within constitutional limits, upholding the rule of law.
  • Guardian of rights: it makes Fundamental Rights enforceable against the State.
  • Federal balance: it settles Centre–State disputes (Art 131) and checked the misuse of Article 356 (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
  • Checks and balances: it prevents a legislative majority from overriding minority rights.

AP angle: In E.V. Chinnaiah v. State of AP (2004) the Supreme Court struck down AP's law sub-categorising Scheduled Castes; a seven-judge bench overruled it in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024), permitting sub-classification.

In conclusion, judicial review keeps every organ within constitutional limits; exercised with judicial restraint and respect for the separation of powers, it strengthens democracy rather than rivalling it.
free.g1m-2023-p3-1a:
Article 19Reasonable restrictionsTest of reasonablenessProportionality

Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms to citizens: speech and expression, peaceful assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession, trade or business (the right to property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978). These freedoms are not absolute. Clauses (2) to (6) allow the State to impose "reasonable restrictions" by law on specified grounds, and the courts, applying the test of reasonableness, decide whether a restriction is valid. The aim is to balance individual liberty with social control.

1. Scope of reasonable restrictions

  • Only on listed grounds: each freedom has its own grounds (see table). In Kaushal Kishore (2023) a Constitution Bench held the grounds in Article 19(2) to be exhaustive, so no new ground can be added by invoking other rights.
  • Only by law: a restriction must be imposed by a valid law, not by an executive instruction (Bijoe Emmanuel, 1986, the national anthem case).
  • Grounds widened by amendment: after Romesh Thappar (1950), the First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence, and inserted the word "reasonable"; the 16th Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity of India.
  • Special situations: Article 33 lets Parliament restrict the rights of the armed forces, and Article 358 suspends Article 19 during an Emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression.

2. The test of reasonableness

  • No fixed standard (V.G. Row, 1952): the court weighs the nature of the right, the purpose of the restriction, the extent and urgency of the evil, proportionality and the prevailing conditions.
  • Not arbitrary or excessive (Chintaman Rao, 1950): a restriction that goes beyond what its object requires is unreasonable.
  • Substance and procedure: both the law and the procedure it lays down must be reasonable; Maneka Gandhi (1978) read Articles 14, 19 and 21 together.
  • Clarity: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as vague and overbroad, separating discussion and advocacy, which are protected, from incitement.

3. Proportionality: the modern test

  • Privacy: Puttaswamy (2017) adopted the test for the right to privacy, and the Aadhaar judgment (2018) applied it to uphold the scheme with limits.
  • Digital age: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) applied proportionality to internet shutdowns: they must be temporary, necessary, published and periodically reviewed.

AP angle: in the protective spirit of Article 19(5), the AP Scheduled Areas Land Transfer Regulation (1 of 1959, amended 1970) bars the transfer of land in Scheduled Areas to non-tribals; in Samatha (1997) the Supreme Court held leases of such land to private mining firms void.

Reasonableness is thus a judicially tested balance: freedom remains the rule and restriction the exception, and proportionality ensures that the State uses the least intrusive means to protect the public interest.
free.g1m-2023-p3-1b:
Article 263Inter-State CouncilSarkaria CommissionCooperative federalism

India's federal system needs forums where the Union and the States can settle friction through dialogue. Article 263 empowers the President to establish an Inter-State Council (ISC), if public interest so requires, to inquire into and advise on disputes between States, investigate subjects of common interest to the Union and States, and recommend better coordination of policy and action. For four decades this provision was not used for a general forum, until the Sarkaria Commission pressed for one.

1. Genesis

  • A dormant provision: until 1990 Article 263 was used only for sectoral advisory bodies such as the Central Council of Health (1952).
  • Demand for a forum: the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-70) and Tamil Nadu's Rajamannar Committee (1969) recommended a standing body for Centre-State consultation.
  • Sarkaria Commission (set up 1983, report 1988): recommended a permanent Inter-State Council under Article 263, which it called the Inter-Governmental Council.
  • Constitution: the ISC was set up by a Presidential Order on 28 May 1990; a Secretariat followed in 1991 and a Standing Committee under the Union Home Minister in 1996.

2. Composition and working

  • Members: the Prime Minister as Chairman, Chief Ministers of all States and of Union Territories with legislatures, Administrators of other UTs, and six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister.
  • Standing Committee: chaired by the Union Home Minister, with some Union Ministers and Chief Ministers, it prepares matters for the Council and follows up its recommendations.
  • Method: it is a recommendatory body; questions are decided by consensus, which suits a forum meant for trust-building.

3. Relevance for coordination and cooperation

  • Neutral platform: issues such as the Governor's role, use of central agencies, river waters, cesses and Centrally Sponsored Schemes need structured dialogue.
  • Policy review: it examined the Sarkaria recommendations and, at its 11th meeting (July 2016), the Punchhi Commission report.
  • Complement to other forums: it works alongside bodies with narrower mandates (see table).

4. Limitations

  • Advisory and irregular: it met only 11 times between 1990 and 2016, and follow-up on its recommendations has been weak.
  • Reform proposals: the Punchhi Commission urged at least three meetings a year to make it a vibrant forum.

AP angle: post-2014 issues between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, such as the division of Schedule IX and X institutions and power dues, are discussed at the Southern Zonal Council and Union Home Ministry meetings; a regularly meeting ISC could settle such issues faster.

A permanent, regularly meeting ISC with a strong secretariat would turn cooperative federalism from a principle into a working habit of dialogue between the Union and the States.
free.g1m-2025-p3-1a:
Emergency provisionsArticle 352Article 356Federal to unitary shift

Part XVIII of the Constitution (Articles 352–360), drawn largely from the Government of India Act 1935, arms the Union with three kinds of emergency powers. They rest on the Union's duty under Article 355 to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance. During an emergency the federal system can turn almost unitary without any formal amendment.

1. Emergency functions of the Union

  • National Emergency (Art 352): proclaimed on war, external aggression or armed rebellion, only on the Union Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment, 1978, which also replaced "internal disturbance"). It was proclaimed in 1962, 1971 and 1975.
  • President's Rule (Art 356): imposed when the constitutional machinery of a State fails, or when a State ignores Union directions (Art 365).
  • Financial Emergency (Art 360): when the financial stability or credit of India or any part of it is threatened; it has never been invoked.
  • Executive control: during a National Emergency the Union can direct a State on any matter (Art 353) and the President can modify the sharing of revenues (Art 354).

2. Impact on the legislative powers of Parliament

  • State List opens up (Art 250): Parliament can make laws on any State subject; such laws lapse six months after the emergency ends.
  • Longer life of the House: Parliament can extend the Lok Sabha's term by one year at a time (Art 83(2)), but not beyond six months after the emergency ends.
  • Rights-restricting laws: Art 19 is suspended during war or external aggression (Art 358), so Parliament can make laws that would otherwise violate it; enforcement of other rights, except Art 20 and 21, may be suspended (Art 359).
  • Ordinances: the President can issue ordinances even on State subjects when Parliament is not in session.

3. Impact on State Legislatures

  • Overridden, not suspended (Art 352): State Legislatures keep functioning, but their laws give way to Parliament's in case of conflict; an Assembly's term can also be extended (Art 172).
  • Suspended or dissolved (Art 356–357): under President's Rule, Parliament legislates for the State, passes its budget or delegates the power to the President; such laws continue until the State Legislature changes them.
  • Money Bills reserved (Art 360): in a Financial Emergency, State Money and Financial Bills may be reserved for the President.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh came under President's Rule in 1973, during the Jai Andhra agitation, and again in 2014 on the eve of bifurcation.

Safeguards: the 44th Amendment let the Lok Sabha end a National Emergency, and S.R. Bommai (1994) made President's Rule subject to judicial review and the floor test.

Emergency powers are a safety valve for national unity, but, as Dr Ambedkar hoped, Art 356 should remain a "dead letter"; the Sarkaria Commission's advice to use it only as a last resort keeps federalism intact.
free.g1m-2025-p3-1b:
Cooperative federalismArticles 256–257Union directionsArticle 365

The Constitution calls India a "Union of States" (Art 1). The Seventh Schedule gives States wide autonomy, yet the framers also placed definite constitutional duties on State Governments, so that 28 States act as parts of one nation rather than as rival units. Granville Austin called this blend of autonomy and obligation cooperative federalism; these duties are its legal backbone.

1. Administrative duties towards the Union

  • Compliance with Union laws (Art 256): a State must use its executive power to ensure that laws made by Parliament are obeyed; the Union may give directions for this. States' police and revenue staff enforce central laws such as the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and the National Food Security Act.
  • Not impeding the Union (Art 257(1)): State executive power must not obstruct the Union's executive power.
  • Communications and railways (Art 257(2)–(3)): when directed, States must maintain means of communication of national or military importance and protect railways in their territory; the Union pays any extra cost (Art 257(4)).
  • Election duty (Art 324(6)): the Governor must make staff available to the Election Commission, which is why State officials conduct Lok Sabha polls.

2. Duties towards other States and the nation

  • Full faith and credit (Art 261): public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State must be recognised throughout India.
  • Inter-State cooperation: States implement river-water tribunal awards (Art 262) and work through the Inter-State Council (Art 263, set up in 1990) and the Zonal Councils.
  • Fiscal discipline (Art 293): a State indebted to the Union needs its consent to borrow; States have Fiscal Responsibility laws, such as the AP FRBM Act 2005.
  • Shared decisions (Art 279A): States sit in the GST Council to keep one national market.

3. Social and democratic duties

  • Directive Principles (Art 37): "fundamental in the governance" of the country, for example panchayats (Art 40), public health (Art 47) and environment (Art 48A).
  • Weaker sections: promote the interests of SCs and STs (Art 46) and follow Union directions on schemes for STs (Art 339(2)).
  • Local democracy (Parts IX and IXA): hold panchayat and municipal elections through a State Election Commission and set up a State Finance Commission every five years.

In return, the Union must protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance (Art 355).

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh executes the Polavaram project, a national project under Section 90 of the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, on the Union's behalf; its State Disaster Management Authority works with the NDRF during cyclones, and it sits in the Southern Zonal Council.

The Sarkaria (1988) and Punchhi (2010) Commissions stressed consultation over coercion: when States perform these duties willingly and the Union respects their autonomy, national unity and State autonomy reinforce each other.
free.g1m-2020-p4-1a:
Make in IndiaPLI schemesEase of doing businessIndustrial corridors

Manufacturing's share in India's GVA has stayed at roughly 15–17% for three decades, well below the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. A weak factory sector means too few jobs for workers leaving farms and a large import bill for electronics and machinery. Since Make in India (September 2014), the government has combined a better investment climate, output-linked incentives and logistics reform to make India a manufacturing hub linked to global value chains.

1. Improving the investment climate

  • Make in India (2014): a campaign covering 25 focus sectors; FDI was liberalised, with the automatic route allowed up to 100% in most sectors and up to 74% in defence (2020).
  • Corporate tax cut (2019): the rate fell to 22% for existing companies and 15% for new manufacturing units set up by March 2024, bringing India in line with competing Asian economies.
  • Regulatory reform: the National Single Window System (2021) for approvals, the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 (minor offences decriminalised), and the four Labour Codes, in force from 21 November 2025, which replace 29 central labour laws.
  • Competitive federalism: State rankings under the Business Reform Action Plan push States to compete for investors.

2. Incentives for scale and technology

  • Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes: 14 sectors with an outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore, including mobiles, pharma, auto, batteries, solar modules, textiles and food. Because support is tied to actual sales, firms are rewarded only when they produce more in India.
  • Semiconductors and electronics: the India Semiconductor Mission (₹76,000 crore, 2021) for fabs and assembly-testing units, and the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme (2025) to deepen the supply chain.
  • National Manufacturing Mission (Union Budget 2025-26): policy support and a roadmap for small, medium and large industry.
  • PM MITRA parks (2021): seven integrated textile parks to give the textile chain scale from fibre to fashion.

3. Infrastructure and logistics

  • PM Gati Shakti (2021): a GIS-based master plan that coordinates roads, railways, ports and gas lines; the National Logistics Policy (2022) aims to cut logistics costs.
  • Dedicated Freight Corridors move cargo faster between the hinterland and ports.
  • Industrial smart cities: 12 new ones under the National Industrial Corridor Programme (August 2024), with ready plots.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

  • Two of these 12 nodes, Orvakal (Kurnool) and Kopparthy (YSR Kadapa), are in AP.
  • The electronics cluster at Sri City, Kia's plant at Penukonda and the State's Industrial Development Policy 4.0 (2024-29) complement the national effort.

The results are visible: smartphones are now among India's largest exports. Raising manufacturing's share further, for Viksit Bharat@2047, needs better skills, more R&D, lower logistics costs and MSMEs linked to global value chains.
free.g1m-2020-p4-1b:
Agricultural productivityFragmented holdingsRain-fed farmingInput and market constraints

Agriculture employs about 46% of India's workers (PLFS 2023-24) but produces less than one-fifth of GVA, which shows low productivity per hectare and per worker. Yields of rice, wheat and pulses are well below those of China and the world leaders. The Green Revolution raised yields mainly in irrigated pockets, while large dryland areas lagged. The causes are structural, technological and institutional, and they reinforce one another.

1. Structural factors

  • Small, fragmented holdings: the average holding is 1.08 ha, and 86% of holdings are small or marginal (Agriculture Census 2015-16). Tiny, scattered plots make tractors, harvesters and borewells uneconomical.
  • Population pressure: too many people depend on the land, so disguised unemployment keeps output per worker low.
  • Insecure tenancy: oral leases leave tenants without bank credit, crop insurance or input subsidies, and without any incentive to invest in land improvement.
  • Low capital formation: public investment in irrigation, drainage and rural infrastructure has lagged behind spending on input subsidies.

2. Technological factors

  • Dependence on the monsoon: nearly half of the net sown area is rain-fed, so a delayed or weak monsoon lowers yields across the dryland belt.
  • Poor inputs: low seed replacement rates, and urea-biased fertiliser use (driven by the subsidy) that is far from the recommended 4:2:1 NPK balance and degrades soil health.
  • Weak research and extension: low spending on agricultural R&D and too few extension workers, so new varieties and practices spread slowly.
  • Low mechanisation on small farms, and little use of precision or protected cultivation.

3. Institutional and market factors

  • Inadequate institutional credit: small and tenant farmers still depend on moneylenders at high interest.
  • Post-harvest losses and volatile prices: poor storage and cold chains, and price crashes that discourage investment in better inputs.
  • Climate change: heat waves, erratic rain and new pests reduce and destabilise yields.

4. Andhra Pradesh angle

The Godavari–Krishna deltas have some of India's highest paddy yields, but rain-fed Rayalaseema, especially drought-prone Anantapur, has low yields. Many delta farmers are tenants, so the AP Crop Cultivators Rights Act, 2019 gives them cards to obtain credit.

Way forward: micro-irrigation (PMKSY, "more crop per drop"), Soil Health Cards, quality seeds, digital agriculture (AgriStack), FPOs and climate-resilient varieties can raise productivity sustainably, a second Green Revolution that is also ecologically sound.
free.g1m-2023-p4-1a:
New Age reformsPublic goodsFormalisationPotential growth

The Economic Survey 2022-23 used the term 'New Age' reforms for the changes made since 2014, which shifted policy from one-time liberalisation to building public goods, formalising the economy and trust-based governance. The Survey compared them with the 1998-2002 reforms that paid off in the 2003-08 boom, and argued that India's medium-term potential growth would rise as their benefits matured.

1. Impact of the reforms

  • Digital public infrastructure: JAM (Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile), Direct Benefit Transfer and UPI (2016) cut leakages and brought millions into formal finance; UPI crossed 20 billion transactions a month in 2025.
  • Tax reform: GST (2017) unified the national market, and the 2019 cut in corporate tax to 22% (15% for new manufacturing units) made India competitive with its Asian peers.
  • Balance-sheet repair: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) and the 4R strategy (recognition, resolution, recapitalisation, reform) cut banks' gross NPAs from 11.2% (March 2018) to about 2.3% (March 2025), reviving credit growth.
  • Macro stability: flexible inflation targeting (2016) and a fiscal glide path helped India absorb COVID-19 and the 2022 commodity shock without a crisis.
  • Investment and ease of business: a public capex push, PM Gati Shakti (2021), PLI schemes (2020), the Jan Vishwas Act 2023 and four Labour Codes (in force from November 2025).

2. Growth potential, 2023-30

The Survey expected average real growth of about 6.5% in the medium term and said potential growth could rise to 7-8% as the reforms pay off. Outcomes so far beat this baseline: 7.4% in 2025-26 (NSO first advance estimate) and an RBI projection of 7.1% for 2026-27 (October 2026).

  • Demographic dividend: a young workforce, if skilled and employed, can lift savings, investment and consumption through the decade.
  • Infrastructure and logistics: record public capex (₹12.2 lakh crore in 2026-27) and Gati Shakti lower logistics costs and crowd in private investment.
  • Global shifts: China-plus-one supply chains, services exports and the digital economy widen the base of growth.
  • Constraints: weak private investment, low female labour force participation (41.7%, PLFS 2023-24), skill gaps, global protectionism and climate risks.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Swarna Andhra@2047 vision likewise counts on ports, industrial corridors, the Amaravati capital and technology-driven governance for high growth.

Sustaining 7-8% growth needs second-generation reforms in land, labour, power and skills, and stronger state capacity: the path to Viksit Bharat@2047.
free.g1m-2023-p4-1b:
Managed floatRupee depreciationImported inflationForex intervention

India follows a managed float. After the dual-rate LERMS of March 1992, the rupee became market-determined in March 1993; the current account was made fully convertible in August 1994, while the capital account remains only partly convertible, as the Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006) advised a cautious path. So the market sets the rate, but the RBI smooths sharp moves.

1. Is the rupee fully market-determined?

  • In principle, yes: there is no official target or band; the rate reflects trade flows, capital flows (FDI, FPI, ECBs), remittances and the interest-rate gap with the US.
  • In practice, managed: the RBI intervenes in spot, forward and offshore (NDF) markets to curb excessive volatility, though it does not defend any particular level.
  • Other levers: capital-account controls, ECB and FPI limits and large reserves (about $700 billion) also shape the rate. The RBI watches the 40-currency REER to judge competitiveness.
  • Verdict: market-determined in principle, managed in practice.

2. Effects of depreciation (from about ₹60 per dollar in 2014 to beyond ₹90 in December 2025)

  • Costlier imports: India imports over 85% of its crude oil, besides edible oils, fertilisers and electronics, so imported inflation and subsidy bills rise.
  • Debt and capital: unhedged firms' foreign borrowings cost more to service, and FPI outflows can become self-reinforcing.
  • Gains: IT services, textiles, pharma and marine exports become more competitive, and remittances (India is the world's largest recipient) are worth more in rupees.
  • Limits: the high import content of exports such as electronics and gems, and the J-curve effect, delay any improvement in the trade balance.

3. Role of the RBI in defending the rupee

  • Direct intervention: selling dollars from reserves in spot and forward markets, and buy-sell swaps to manage the resulting rupee liquidity.
  • Interest rates: the repo rate was raised by 250 bps in 2022-23 and again to 5.50% in October 2026; besides fighting inflation, this narrows the rate gap that drives outflows.
  • Attracting inflows: in 2013 a special FCNR(B) swap window drew about $34 billion; in July 2022 the RBI relaxed interest caps on FCNR(B) and NRE deposits, raised the ECB limit and eased FPI norms.
  • Less dollar dependence: rupee trade settlement through Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (2022) and a local-currency arrangement with the UAE (2023).

AP angle: a weaker rupee helps Andhra Pradesh's shrimp and rice exporters but raises costs for Visakhapatnam's crude-importing refinery and pharma units that import raw materials.

The RBI should smooth volatility, not defend a level; lasting rupee stability needs a lower current account deficit, stronger exports and steady capital inflows.
free.g1m-2025-p4-1a:
Current Account DeficitBalance of PaymentsTrade deficitRupee depreciation

The Balance of Payments (BoP) records all of India's transactions with the rest of the world. Its current account covers trade in goods and services, income and transfers; a Current Account Deficit (CAD) arises when payments exceed receipts and must be financed by capital inflows or by drawing down reserves. India's CAD was about 0.6% of GDP in 2025-26 (US$25.2 billion, RBI), but a much wider goods deficit and volatile capital flows kept the BoP under pressure.

1. Factors contributing to the CAD

  • Large merchandise trade deficit: India imports over 85% of its crude oil, besides gold, electronics, coal and fertilisers; the goods deficit (BoP basis) widened to US$337.3 billion in 2025-26 from US$286.9 billion in 2024-25 (RBI).
  • Narrow export base: weak manufacturing competitiveness, a small role in global value chains and a trade deficit of about US$99 billion with China (2024-25).
  • External shocks: volatile crude prices (West Asia conflict, 2026) and US tariff actions in 2025 hurt exports such as shrimp, textiles and gems.
  • Primary income outflows: interest on external debt, and dividends and profits repatriated by foreign firms.

2. Why the BoP turned unfavourable

  • Weak capital inflows: in 2025-26, net FPI outflows of US$16.4 billion and net FDI of only US$6.9 billion left the CAD unfinanced, so foreign-exchange reserves fell by US$23.6 billion on a BoP basis (RBI).
  • Rupee depreciation: the rupee breached ₹90 per US dollar in December 2025.
  • Cushions: a large services surplus (US$216.6 billion in 2025-26, from IT and Global Capability Centres) and record remittances (about US$135 billion in 2024-25) keep the CAD far smaller than the goods deficit.

3. Implications for the Indian economy

  • Imported inflation: a weaker rupee and costlier crude raise fuel and input costs; rising inflation led the RBI to raise the repo rate to 5.50% in October 2026.
  • Reserves and liquidity: RBI's dollar sales to steady the rupee use up reserves and tighten domestic liquidity; external borrowing becomes costlier to service.
  • Sustainability: a CAD below about 2.5% of GDP is considered manageable; the 4.8% CAD of 2012-13 left India exposed in the 2013 taper tantrum, and the 1991 crisis followed a collapse of reserves.
  • Twin deficits: a high fiscal deficit adds to import demand and widens the CAD.

AP angle: AP's merchandise exports were ₹1.59 lakh crore in 2025-26 (DGCI&S data), with marine products at 18%, so US tariffs on shrimp directly hurt the State's aquaculture farmers.

Export diversification through FTAs (India–UK CETA, 2025; India–EFTA TEPA), PLI-led manufacturing and an energy transition that cuts oil imports can make India's external sector resilient.
free.g1m-2025-p4-1b:
ManufacturingInfrastructure bottlenecksLogistics costPM Gati Shakti

Manufacturing contributes only about 17% of India's GVA, well short of the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. Factories compete on cost and time, and both depend on infrastructure: power, transport, ports, land and water. Costly and unreliable infrastructure therefore acts as a hidden tax that keeps Indian firms small and less competitive than rivals in East and South-East Asia.

1. How infrastructure bottlenecks hinder manufacturing

  • High logistics cost: estimated at 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT, for 2021-22); freight is road-heavy and railways carry only about 27% of it, raising costs for bulk goods such as steel and cement.
  • Power: industrial tariffs carry cross-subsidies for farm and household users; DISCOM losses and interruptions push firms to costly captive power and diesel back-up.
  • Ports and last-mile links: congestion, weak hinterland rail and road links and slow multimodal transfer raise turnaround time and inventory costs, hurting time-sensitive exports.
  • Land: difficult acquisition, fragmented holdings and few plug-and-play industrial parks delay projects for years.
  • Other gaps: water scarcity, urban congestion, and weak testing, certification and R&D facilities for MSMEs.

2. Impact on the sector

  • Small scale: high costs keep most firms small and informal, unable to reap economies of scale.
  • Weak exports: costs and delays limit India's integration into global value chains.
  • Low investment: uncertainty over land and power deters private capex and FDI in labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and footwear.
  • Lost jobs: labour-intensive factories need cheap logistics and reliable power; where these are lacking, investment goes to competitors such as Vietnam and Bangladesh, a lost opportunity for India's young workforce.

3. Steps to address them

  • States' role: land and water are State subjects and power is distributed by State DISCOMs, so single-window clearances, land banks and DISCOM reforms are essential.
  • Regulatory ease: decriminalisation under the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 and faster dispute resolution remove non-physical bottlenecks.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh hosts two of the new industrial smart cities, Orvakal and Kopparthy; the Visakhapatnam–Chennai and Chennai–Bengaluru industrial corridors and new ports at Ramayapatnam, Machilipatnam and Mulapeta aim to cut logistics costs for its industries.

Cheap and reliable power, seamless multimodal logistics and ready industrial land, planned jointly by the Centre and the States, can lift manufacturing's share and make India a global manufacturing hub.
free.g1m-2020-p5-1a:
Life expectancy at birthMortality declineHealth transitionPublic health

Life expectancy at birth is the average number of years a newborn would live if the age-specific death rates of a given period stayed unchanged throughout its life. It summarises the health of a whole population rather than predicting any one person's lifespan. Globally it has risen from about 32 years in 1900 to 73.3 years in 2024 (UN World Population Prospects 2024); India's rose from about 32 years in 1951 to a little over 70 years today.

1. Why it matters as an indicator

  • Captures deaths at every age: a death in infancy removes many potential years, so falling child mortality lifts the average far more than gains in old age.
  • Measure of development: it is one of the three dimensions of the UNDP's Human Development Index and reflects nutrition, sanitation and health care together.

2. Factors behind the improvement

  • Vaccines and control of infections: smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 and India became polio-free in 2014; the Universal Immunisation Programme (1985) and Mission Indradhanush protect children from measles, diphtheria, tetanus and severe forms of TB.
  • Clean water and sanitation: sewers and chlorinated water cut cholera and typhoid in 19th-century Europe; in India, Swachh Bharat (2014) and the Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water in about 82% of rural homes by July 2026) play the same role.
  • Medicines and medical technology: antibiotics after penicillin (1928), oral rehydration salts for diarrhoea, anti-malarials and TB drugs, and later treatment for heart disease, diabetes and cancer.
  • Better nutrition and food security: the Green Revolution, the public distribution system, the National Food Security Act (2013) and mid-day meals prevented famines and reduced child undernutrition.
  • Mother-and-child care and wider development: institutional deliveries (about 89% of births, NFHS-5) and newborn care have brought India's infant mortality to 24 per 1,000 and maternal mortality to 87 per lakh live births (SRS); income growth, female literacy and smaller families reinforce these gains.

3. Challenges that remain

  • Quality of years: non-communicable diseases now cause about two-thirds of deaths in India; air pollution and drug resistance threaten healthy years.
  • Inequality: infant mortality ranges from 8 in Kerala to 36 in Chhattisgarh (SRS 2024), and rural rates exceed urban ones.
  • Shocks: COVID-19 cut global life expectancy in 2020–21; it has returned to pre-pandemic levels in nearly all countries since 2022 (UN, 2024).
  • Ageing: more elderly people need pensions, geriatric care and long-term support.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's maternal mortality ratio of 30 (2021–23) is the joint lowest in India with Kerala; Dr NTR Vaidya Seva gives cashless hospital care, and a Universal Health Policy approved in 2025 aims to widen it.

The doubling of life expectancy owes more to public health (vaccines, water, food and safe births) than to hospitals alone. The next goal is to add healthy years, through prevention of chronic disease, clean air and universal health coverage.
free.g1m-2023-p5-1a:
Knowledge creation vs consumptionScientific Social ResponsibilityLab-to-society gapScientific temper

India creates knowledge at scale: it is third in the world in scientific publications and received over 1.1 lakh patent applications in 2024-25. Yet much of this stays in journals and laboratories, unused by farmers, small industries, schools or policymakers. Scientific Social Responsibility (SSR), the duty of scientists to share knowledge, facilities and skills with society, was formalised by DST's SSR Guidelines, 2022. The statement is largely valid, with one caveat.

1. Stand: largely agree, with a caveat

  • Lab-to-market gap: much publicly funded research ends as papers; university patents are rarely licensed, and MSMEs and farmers seldom use technologies that already exist.
  • Lab-to-society gap: superstition, quackery, vaccine hesitancy and misinformation persist despite the fundamental duty to develop scientific temper (Article 51A(h)), so knowledge is not "consumed" by society.
  • But creation also lags: R&D spending is only 0.84% of GDP (2023-24) against China's 2.58%, and India has just 354 researchers per million people. SSR complements, but cannot replace, more research funding.

2. How SSR can remedy the situation

  • Knowledge sharing: scientists give public lectures, train teachers, mentor students and explain research in local languages; the guidelines ask for at least 10 days of SSR a year, credited in performance appraisal.
  • Sharing facilities: laboratories open costly instruments to colleges, start-ups and MSMEs that cannot afford them.
  • Demand-driven research: contact with farmers, fishers and local bodies helps scientists pick real problems; the CSIR Aroma Mission (Vigyan Team award, 2025) took aromatic crops and distillation to farmers.
  • Trust and scientific temper: CSIR's Jigyasa (student–scientist connect) and Unnat Bharat Abhiyan (institutions adopting villages) build a culture of inquiry.

3. Challenges in implementing SSR

  • Non-binding guidelines: SSR is voluntary, so institutions apply it unevenly.
  • Incentives and workload: promotions still reward papers and grants; teaching-heavy state universities have little spare time.
  • No dedicated funds: travel, outreach and instrument-sharing costs lack a budget line.
  • Measuring impact: counting hours is easy, judging real social benefit is hard, so SSR risks becoming box-ticking.
  • Language and access: most science is in English, while rural and tribal users need field-level, local-language communication.

AP angle: APCOST (Vijayawada), IIT and IISER Tirupati, NARL Gadanki and ANGRAU can anchor SSR through school adoption, farmer outreach and shared laboratories, with the Ratan Tata Innovation Hub (2025) linking them to start-ups.

SSR turns science from an ivory-tower activity into a public good. Backed by funds, appraisal credit and impact measures, and by higher R&D spending through ANRF, it can make India both a creator and a user of knowledge.
free.g1m-2023-p5-1b:
Digital healthAyushman Bharat Digital MissionTelemedicineAI in healthcare

India's health system faces a triple challenge: too few doctors and specialists in rural areas, a rising burden of non-communicable diseases alongside TB and infections, and high out-of-pocket spending, because public spending is still below the 2.5% of GDP target of the National Health Policy, 2017. Technology, from digital health IDs and telemedicine to AI, genomics and drones, can stretch scarce resources and bring care closer to people.

1. Matching technology to India's health challenges

2. How technology is transforming healthcare

  • Access: e-Sanjeevani offers doctor-to-doctor and online OPD consultations where specialists are absent; Tele-MANAS (14416) gives 24×7 mental-health support in many languages.
  • Continuity and efficiency: the ABHA ID lets records follow the patient; ABDM's Scan and Share OPD tokens (over 23 crore by June 2026) cut registration waits from about an hour to a few minutes.
  • Public-health intelligence: CoWIN managed over 220 crore COVID-19 doses, U-WIN records routine immunisation, and the Integrated Health Information Platform tracks outbreaks.
  • Precision and lower costs: the government's AI strategy for healthcare (SAHI) and the BODH benchmarking platform (February 2026), Genome India's 10,000 genomes and indigenous devices cut costs and import dependence.
  • Financial protection: PM-JAY's IT platform runs cashless, portable treatment: over 48.5 crore Ayushman cards and 13.25 crore admissions by August 2026.

3. Limitations and concerns

  • Digital divide: only about half of women used a mobile phone of their own (NFHS-5); the elderly, poor and tribal people need assisted access.
  • Privacy and security: health data are highly sensitive; the DPDP Act, 2023 must be enforced, and the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi (2022) showed the risk.
  • No substitute for staff: teleconsultation needs working health centres, drugs and tests; AI must be validated on Indian data, with clear accountability for errors.
  • Uneven adoption: many private providers are yet to link records, and high-end therapies remain costly.

AP angle: AIIMS Mangalagiri, the AP MedTech Zone at Visakhapatnam (India's first medical-devices park, 2016), the cashless Dr NTR Vaidya Seva network and the proposed Universal Health Policy (2025) can use digital records and telemedicine to reach tribal and Rayalaseema areas.

Technology is a force multiplier, not a replacement, for doctors, nurses and public spending. With stronger primary care, data protection and digital literacy, it can carry India towards universal health coverage (SDG 3.8) by 2030.
free.g1m-2025-p5-1b:
Internet of ThingsSmart homeHome automationCyber security

The Internet of Things (IoT), a term coined by Kevin Ashton in 1999, is a network of everyday objects fitted with sensors, chips and internet connectivity that collect data and act on it with little human input. In homes, it links electricity meters, lights, locks, cameras, pumps and appliances to phones, voice assistants and the cloud, turning a house into a smart home. Cheap sensors, home broadband and 5G (launched October 2022) have spread it rapidly in India.

1. How home automation works

2. Impact on household systems

  • Energy: prepaid smart meters show real-time use, end manual meter reading and allow mobile recharges; smart plugs and timers cut waste. India had installed 7.24 crore smart meters by 30 June 2026, 5.73 crore of them under the RDSS (Rajya Sabha reply, July 2026).
  • Safety and security: app-linked CCTV, video doorbells, smart locks and smoke or gas-leak sensors raise instant alerts, even when the family is away.
  • Water: level sensors start and stop motor pumps, ending overflowing tanks, while soil-moisture sensors water gardens only when needed.
  • Health and elderly care: wearables track heart rate, sleep and falls and alert relatives or doctors, helping elderly people live independently.
  • Convenience: voice assistants control lights, fans and TVs; robot vacuum cleaners and scheduled washing machines save time.

3. How everyday tasks have evolved

4. Concerns: an evaluation

  • Privacy: cameras, speakers and meters record voices, images and daily habits; the DPDP Act, 2023 (Rules notified November 2025, most duties from May 2027) gives users rights over such data.
  • Cyber security: devices with default passwords are easy to hack; in 2016 the Mirai botnet hijacked cameras and routers to knock major websites offline. CERT-In and the Cyber Swachhta Kendra help detect and clean such infections.
  • Cost and digital divide: smart homes are mostly urban and affluent and need reliable power and internet.
  • Interoperability and e-waste: devices of different brands often do not work together, and short-lived gadgets add to e-waste.
  • Over-dependence: a server or network outage can lock users out of their own devices.

AP angle: by 30 June 2026 Andhra Pradesh had installed about 32.8 lakh of the 59.2 lakh smart meters sanctioned under RDSS, about 31.4 lakh of them at consumers' premises, and AP Fibernet carries low-cost broadband and IPTV to homes.

On balance, IoT has moved household work from manual, reactive chores to automated, data-driven services that save energy, time and even lives. Secure-by-design devices, strong data protection and affordable access must go with it, so that smart homes are also safe homes.
